An agent story · five lessons, one local model, 2026
Can I build an AI agent from scratch, and prove it works?
A work log agent in plain Python, on a free model running on my own PC, tested with known right answers at every step.
Scott Schirkofsky · schirko.com/scott/agentic-engineering-worklog
The goal
Turn one plain-English sentence into a saved record.
What I type
“Fixed the alert email bug in Cornerpost Watch for about 2 hours.”
What gets saved
project: Cornerpost Watch
description: Fixed the alert email bug
hours: 2
Then answer questions about it later, such as “How many hours have I logged on Herd Planner today?” It's the base for a productivity app I want to build.
The sentence is from lesson 2's test set; the record is copied from the saved log file.
2
What agentic engineering means
AI does much of the work. A person decides what's built and proves it's right.
The loose version
Vibe coding
Describe what you want, let the AI write it, and move on if it seems to work. Fast, and fine for experiments. The question is “does it look right?”
The disciplined version
Agentic engineering
The same AI help, plus checks: write down what it should do, review the plan, build in small steps, prove it with tests. The question is “what proves it's right?”
Specify
I decide
Plan
the agent drafts
Implement
the agent builds
Verify
I check
This project does both senses: engineering with an AI agent, and engineering an agent.

The setup
A free model on a home PC: no API bill, and nothing leaves the machine.
8B
parameters: qwen3:8b, a model small enough to run at home
100%
of its 5.9 GB in memory sits on two GTX 1060 6 GB video cards
17.5
tokens per second while writing, in lesson 1's saved run
$0
per call: it runs through Ollama, with no paid API key
The trade-off: it's slower and less capable than large hosted models, so every weakness shows. That makes it a good teacher.
Lesson 1, Steps 3 and 4. A token is a short word or piece of a word; 100 tokens is about 75 words.

Lesson 1 · One model call
The model keeps nothing between calls, and invents what it doesn't know.
It forgets
Call 1
I spent this morning on my Cornerpost Watch project.
Call 2
Which project did I work on this morning?
I don't have access to your personal work history or calendar.
Sent along with call 1, the same question got the right answer.
It invents
Asked to reply “LOGGED: project | what was done”
Spent an hour cleaning the meat price data.
LOGGED: Meat Price Data | Cleaned the meat price data.
No project by that name exists, and nothing was saved. It only looked like a record.

Lesson 3 · The loop
Let it keep using tools until the job is done. That's an agent.
1
Send the messages and the tools to the model
2
It asks for tools; my code runs them
3
Send the results back
4
Repeat until it answers, at most 6 steps
Log 1 hour on Herd Planner updating the calving chart, then tell me how many hours I've logged on Herd Planner today.
step 1: add_entry(project='Herd Planner', hours=1)
step 1: search_entries(project='Herd Planner', date_from='2026-11-16')
step 2: answered
You have logged 2 hours on Herd Planner today.
6 of 6 on tools, answers and saved entries. It asked for both tools at once, save first and search second. Totals are added up in code, so the model only repeats a finished number.
From lesson 3's saved output. Tool arguments shortened; the full calls are in the notebook.
7
When to use an agent
Most tasks don't need an agent. I climb only when the problem forces it.
Step 1
Plain code
The rules can be written down. “Flag animals whose withdrawal date is after today” is a date comparison.
Step 2
One model call
Fixed steps, but one needs language. Turning “gave tag 214 her booster today” into a record. Lesson 2.
Step 3
An agent
The next step depends on what the last one found, so the steps can't be written in advance. Lesson 3.
Agents are slower, less predictable and harder to test, so each one needs limits and a test set.

Memory works, and every turn costs more to read.
+62%
more to read by turn 5 than turn 1, because every earlier turn is sent again
A surprise
“Actually, make that two hours” worked with no memory at all: the correction tool reads the last entry from the log file.
Tokens the model read at the start of each turn of one conversation. From lesson 4's saved output.

Lesson 5 · The control test
Same six tests, run twice: with memory, and with it switched off.
6 of 6
passed with memory
2 of 6

4
tests that really depend on memory
Lesson 4 also scored 6 of 6, but most of its tests would have passed without memory. A control is what shows what a score really measures.
From lesson 5's saved output: each test run with max_turns=5, then max_turns=0.
10
What went wrong without memory
Without the information it needs, it guesses instead of asking.
Earlier: “My main project this week is Herd Planner.”
“Log 3 hours on my main project.”
With no memory, it saved 3 hours to Cornerpost Watch, the first name on its project list. Lesson 4's version of this test used Cornerpost Watch, so it passed by luck.
Earlier: “Everything I log next is for Cornerpost Logic.”
“Spent 2 hours on the company site.”
With no memory, it saved 2 hours to Agentic Engineering Worklog, and gave no warning.
A guess gets saved as if it were fact. Memory fixes these cases; asking when the project isn't clear would fix the rest.
From lesson 5's saved output, the runs with memory switched off.

> python -m worklog --once "Spent 30 minutes on the Cornerpost Logic company site."
[step 1] add_entry(project='Cornerpost Logic', hours=0.5)
Agent: The entry for Cornerpost Logic has been saved.
> python -m worklog --once "How many hours have I logged today?"
[step 1] search_entries(date_from='2026-11-20', date_to='2026-11-20')
Agent: Today, you have logged a total of 4 hours.
Two separate runs share no memory. The second still got the right total, 4 hours, because it searched the log file the first one wrote.
From lesson 5's saved output. 389 lines in all, many of them comments and descriptions.
12
What I learned
Five things I'd tell anyone building their first agent.
1
The model only knows what you send it. Memory is a list of messages, and your code controls it.
2
Give it real tools and exact work. Code saves the record and adds up the hours.
3
Saved data is more reliable than memory. The log file handled corrections on its own.
4
A test needs a control. Switch the feature off and see what still passes.
5
When it lacks information, it guesses. And the guess gets saved as fact.
